title: One Ticket, 800 Years
logline: One Yellow Line ride from Chandni Chowk to Qutab Minar carries Delhi forward from Shah Jahan's city of 1639 to 1931 and 1947, then turns the clock back through the Tughlaq and Tomar ruins to the Qutb of around 1199 and an iron pillar older than any of them - a city that keeps being rebuilt by people who arrive.

claims.text: The film frames a single metro ticket as the way into the city's long history; this is the maker's own title framing.
In 1639 Shah Jahan chose a site for a new capital, Shahjahanabad, today's Old Delhi, and began building the Red Fort.
The Red Fort straddles the eastern fringes of Chandni Chowk, the old street market.
Jahanara Begum, Shah Jahan's eldest daughter, laid out Chandni Chowk with a sarai and gardens; a canal ran down its middle and an octagonal pool reflected the moonlight.
Tradition gives Chandni Chowk its name from the moonlight reflected in that pool.
Shah Jahan's Jama Masjid was completed in 1656.
About five thousand workers built the Jama Masjid.
Jantar Mantar, near Patel Chowk station, was completed in 1724.
Jantar Mantar is an observatory of astronomical instruments for measuring the harmony of the heavens.
New Delhi was formally inaugurated as the capital on 13 February 1931 by the Viceroy.
Up to 23,000 labourers worked on the Viceroy's House at the peak of construction.
The Viceroy's House is now Rashtrapati Bhavan.
About half a million refugees entered Delhi after Partition.
Many of Delhi's Muslims left the city after Partition, so people moved in both directions.
Malviya Nagar was among the new colonies laid out to rehouse Partition refugees.
The new colonies were planned with their own markets, schools, temples and gurdwaras.
From Chandni Chowk to Saket the Yellow Line runs underground, and the train comes up into daylight only as it nears Qutab Minar.
The Qutb Minar was begun around 1199 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak.
Iltutmish completed the Qutb Minar.
Iltutmish made Delhi the capital of the sultanate.
The iron pillar stands in the Qutb complex and dates from the 5th century.
The pillar resists rust because its iron is rich in phosphorus; a thin protective layer forms next to the metal and greatly slows corrosion.
Delhi is a city of arrivals: by 2011 about four in ten people living there had last lived in another state or country.

After Partition, new colonies were laid out for refugees with their own markets, schools, temples and gurdwaras, and many of Delhi's own Muslims left in the other direction, more than half of those resettled by the Ministry of Rehabilitation going into homes left behind by departing Muslims.

director.logline: One Yellow Line ride from Chandni Chowk to Qutab Minar carries Delhi from Shah Jahan's city of 1639 forward to the republic of 1931 and 1947, then backward through the Tughlaq and Tomar ruins to the Qutb of about 1199 and an iron pillar older than any of them - the story of a city that keeps being rebuilt by people who arrive.
director.hook: Sit down, traveller. One ticket buys you eight hundred years.
director.time_direction: The dates do not run one way along this ride, and the film will say so out loud. The first leg moves forward in time: Shahjahanabad (founded 1639, inaugurated 1648), the Jama Masjid (1656), Jantar Mantar (1724), New Delhi inaugurated (1931), the Partition colonies (1947-50). Then, after Malviya Nagar, the clock runs backwards: Khirki Masjid (1351), the Qutb Minar begun around 1199, and an iron pillar of the 5th century. So no stop here is simply older than the stop before it - some are much younger - and the narrator will name the direction of the years as we go, never claiming each stop takes us further into the past.

stops.why: The ride begins inside Shah Jahan's new capital on the Yamuna: the fort founded 1639 and inaugurated 1648, and the street Jahanara laid out with a canal and a pool, whose traditional name means moonlight square. The same gates that carry 1648 also carry 1857, and the narration will say so without blaming anyone.

Two layers in one stop: the city's faith in stone - Shah Jahan's mosque, foundation 1650, five thousand workers, finished 1656 - and the modern layer, because from here the train runs underground under the old heart and only surfaces near the terminus. The bazaar below the mosque keeps the everyday Delhi of the street.

Continuing the forward run of the clock: a gurdwara of 1664 and the stone observatory of giant instruments built in 1724, proof that this city kept measuring the sky and the seasons, and kept receiving new arrivals to pray in them.

The great leap forward in time, and the hinge of the film: at the 1911 Durbar the capital of British India was moved to Delhi; building began in 1912; on 13 February 1931 New Delhi was formally inaugurated, with the Viceroy's House of some 340 rooms put up by tens of thousands of labourers. Indian names stand on top of it now.

Where the film turns from time to people. This is one of the new colonies laid out after Partition, when about half a million refugees arrived and about 330,000 of the city's Muslims left - movement in both directions - and where a mosque from 1351 still stands, the first hint that the years are about to run backwards.

stops.era: c.1199, and the 5th century before it
stops.why: The oldest stone the line reaches: the tower begun around 1199 by Qutb ud-Din Aibak and finished by Iltutmish, later repaired after a lightning strike, UNESCO-listed in 1993 - and beside it an iron pillar of the 5th century, about six tons, whose phosphorus-rich metal has slowed its rust for sixteen centuries. The film's title and its promise are cashed here.

arc.purpose: The ride itself: the line goes underground under the old heart, the years first run forward and then turn back, and each stop lights up one layer of the city.
beats: Underground from Chandni Chowk to the last station before daylight - the line's own history (2004 first underground section, 2005 under the old city, 2010 south to Qutab Minar).
Forward in time: Shahjahanabad founded 1639, inaugurated 1648; the moonlight street laid out by Jahanara; the Jama Masjid finished 1656; Jantar Mantar 1724.
Then the clock leaps forward to 1931: the 1911 announcement, Lutyens' New Delhi, Rashtrapati Bhavan with tens of thousands of labourers at the peak.
Honest turn, said aloud: 'here I turn the clock back' - Khirki Masjid 1351, Qutb Minar c.1199, and an iron pillar from the 5th century that will not rust.

arc.purpose: The city as a place of arrivals: Partition moved people in both directions, the Games brought workers from other states, the hills sent sons for work, and the arrivals kept coming.
beats: 1947: about half a million refugees arrived, about 330,000 Muslims left; tents became colonies such as Malviya Nagar; forts and tombs served as camps in both directions.
1982: workers from Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha built the Asian Games city, and in 1982 India's Supreme Court held that paying below the minimum wage can be forced labour.

rejected.reason: Accuracy trap: the Peshori Lal Lamba / Kwality Partition story is contradicted by The Week (the restaurant predates Partition). Not used.
Source was a reader's highlight of Dalrymple rather than the book; the Ramlila-at-Zafar detail is too risky to put on screen.
Ramlila committee founding dates conflict across sources and would be on-screen trivia; the Ramlila Maidan reference is dropped.
Indraprastha is tradition, not evidence, and a 1400 BCE frame would break the film's 800-year promise and its map logic.
Purana Qila excavation detail (nine cultural levels, 2,500 years) is too technical and needs a stop that does not exist on this ride.
Stratified PGW finds from 2023-24 are not confirmed in the evidence; the 900 BCE / 540 BCE dating would also overreach the title.
Asiad flyover counts are unverified (5-7 in secondary sources, PIB figure not tied to Asiad), so the flyover line is kept vague.
The Koh-i-Noor adds loot drama the film does not need; fact_089's 1739 sacking can carry the destruction in one clause without a diamond.
The 1858 demolition estimate ('about a third') is one tourism figure and would compete with the 1857 line for space; one war beat only.
The 2018 UN ranking and its 2028 projection are superseded by the 2025 figures and would put a stale number on screen.
1981 and 1991 census pair duplicates the 1941-51 growth fact; dropped to protect word budget.
India Gate's 13,000 inscribed names and the 1914-19 dedication is lovely but the 1931 inauguration and Rashtrapati Bhavan carry the New Delhi stop better.
The Delhi Triangle framing is a strong map device but the triangle's edges are not narratable facts for this ride; dropped from the narration.

risks: Do not claim the stops get older as the train goes south. The first leg runs forward (1639-48, 1656, 1724, 1931, 1947); only from Malviya Nagar southward do the years run back (1351, c.1199, 5th century). The narrator will say the direction out loud.
Qutb Minar: say 'begun around 1199' / 'c. 1199', never 'in 1199'. Height 72.5 m only if used.
The station is not at the monument: the tower is about 1.3 km from Qutab Minar station. Never say the minar can be seen from the platform, and never call it 'a short walk'.

Iron pillar: it resists rust because its iron is rich in phosphorus; it still corrodes extremely slowly. Never say 'rustproof'. Identify Chandra with Chandragupta II as an identification, not a certainty.

Partition: say both directions - about half a million refugees came in, about 330,000 Muslims left - and use 'about'/'around', since these are estimates. Never draw or mention borders on the map, and never show the camps as only for arrivals from one side.

1857: keep the language factual and blameless - a siege, a gate blown with gunpowder, the city recaptured, both sides killing - and never name the contested term as fact or show any living or historical person.

[personal memory removed at the maker's request] Never say the family worked on the Asian Games sites - the Supreme Court judgment names Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and Orissa. [personal memory removed at the maker's request]
[personal memory removed at the maker's request] Say 'by' the stadium, never 'inside' it.
[personal memory removed at the maker's request] The safe claim is that it is loved here and that Partition-era cooks shaped how Delhi eats.

No living people by name, image or likeness: no modern politicians, no living architect of the Asian Games Village, no living historian. Jawaharlal Nehru and George V are long dead and may be named only if essential; better to say 'the Viceroy' and 'the King'.
Yellow Line claims: about 37 stations and roughly 47 km; about eighteen lakh boardings a day with the heaviest rush-hour load in the network - never 'the busiest line'.

Captions use current names: 'Seva Teerth' (formerly Udyog Bhawan, renamed 2026), 'Lok Kalyan Marg' (renamed 2016, not 2017), 'Qutab Minar' for the station and 'Qutb Minar' for the monument, 'Millennium City Centre Gurugram'.
Master Plan: call it the Master Plan for Delhi 2047, notified in the Gazette in August 2026 - never '2041'.
No text, lettering, signs, logos or flags in any illustration; no recognisable real faces; no national borders on the map - only the city, the Yamuna and the line.

accuracy.note: Dates are hedged correctly (1639 founded, 1648 inaugurated, c. 1199), Partition is told in both directions, the pillar is never called rustproof, no living people are named or shown, and no borders appear. Two things still nag: the 'oldest thing the line reaches' is now the 5th-century pillar rather than the 1199 tower, and the claim that Delhi 'has always been a city of arrivals' is asserted from the city rather than from the census evidence in the pack. I have moved that line into the personal scene and tied it to Census 2011 in the claims.
